clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive GM2 gangliosidosis caused by deficiency of both hexosaminidase A and hexosaminidase B, due to pathogenic variants in the HEXB gene encoding the shared beta subunit
It closely resembles Tay-Sachs disease clinically, with infantile onset of developmental regression, hypotonia, an exaggerated startle response, and a cherry-red macular spot
Unlike Tay-Sachs disease, visceral involvement such as hepatosplenomegaly and mild skeletal changes can occur, reflecting the additional deficiency of hexosaminidase B
Progressive macrocephaly, seizures, spasticity, and blindness follow, with death usually in early childhood in the infantile form
Juvenile and adult-onset forms exist with slower motor, cerebellar, and psychiatric presentations
The absence of both hexosaminidase isoenzymes on assay distinguishes it biochemically from Tay-Sachs disease, in which hexosaminidase B is preserved
It is not restricted to any single ethnic group, unlike the increased Tay-Sachs carrier frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population
No disease-modifying therapy is established, so management is supportive with genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Sandhoff disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in HEXB, encoding the beta subunit common to both hexosaminidase A (alpha-beta) and hexosaminidase B (beta-beta). Loss of the beta subunit therefore reduces activity of both isoenzymes, impairing degradation of GM2 ganglioside and related glycolipids and glycoproteins. GM2 accumulates within neuronal lysosomes, driving progressive neurodegeneration, while the broader substrate accumulation from combined enzyme loss also affects visceral tissues, producing organomegaly not typically seen in Tay-Sachs disease.
additionalDifferentials: Niemann-Pick disease and other storage disorders with organomegaly
Other causes of infantile neurodegeneration with cherry-red spot
additionalInvestigations: Assay of hexosaminidase A and total hexosaminidase activity, showing deficiency of both
HEXB molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Ophthalmological examination for the macular cherry-red spot
Assessment for visceral involvement and carrier testing of relatives
redFlags: Rapid developmental regression with exaggerated startle in an infant
Emerging seizures or loss of vision
Progressive swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: The infantile form is progressive and fatal, typically within the first few years of life. Juvenile and adult forms progress more slowly with a variable course. Care remains supportive, as no disease-modifying therapy is established.
pitfalls: Assuming Tay-Sachs disease without recognising that combined hexosaminidase A and B deficiency indicates Sandhoff disease
Overlooking organomegaly as a distinguishing feature from Tay-Sachs disease
Not offering carrier screening and counselling to at-risk families
Attributing the exaggerated startle to a benign cause and delaying evaluation
management: Supportive, symptom-directed care as no disease-modifying therapy is established for this GM2 gangliosidosis
Antiepileptic drugs for the seizures that emerge with disease progression
Antispasticity agents and physiotherapy for spasticity and to prevent contractures
Nutritional and feeding support, including gastrostomy feeding as bulbar function fails
Respiratory care with management of secretions and aspiration risk
Physiotherapy, developmental support and early integration of palliative care for the progressive infantile form
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive HEXB disorder, with carrier testing of relatives and reproductive options
Coordinated multidisciplinary care across metabolic medicine, neurology and community paediatric services
